flags.quote: Moving your pawn to g6 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: This is the King's Indian. g6 exists to fianchetto the bishop, not because a random pawn nudge is 'the strongest move' with zero reason. I already know I pushed a pawn; tell me I am making a home for the bishop and fighting for the long diagonal.

flags.quote: Moving your f8-bishop to g7 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: The only tagged reason is development, and the sentence does not even use it. This is the move the whole opening is named for. If you cannot say 'fianchetto' or 'long diagonal,' at least do not dress a book developing move as a unique engine gift.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to d6 is the strongest move because you put more pressure on the center.
flags.critique: d6 does not pressure the center; it supports ...e5 or ...c5 and unblocks the bishop. 'Pressure on the center' is the same phrase-bank line you already used for Nf6 and c4. I stop believing you.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to c5 is the strongest move because you put more pressure on the center.
flags.critique: This is the Benoni-style break against d4. The lesson is the pawn strike and the fight for d4, not another spin of 'pressure on the center.' Identical because-clause to d6 two plies ago.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to d5 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: White just locked the center and turned this into a Benoni structure. That is the whole strategic fork of the game, and you gave me a blank verdict. Teach space, the closed center, or why d5 rather than taking on c5.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to h3 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: h3 asks the g4-bishop what it wants. That is a pawn kicking a piece, and you already have kicked_by_pawn in the pipeline — just not as a benefit of the kicker. Empty 'strongest move' on the move that forces the trade is coaching malpractice.

flags.quote: Taking the knight on f3 with your g4-bishop is the strongest move because you pin the bishop to the queen and you take the defender of the white pawn.
flags.critique: I captured a knight that h3 just attacked. The 'pin the bishop to the queen' is a one-ply ghost on e2 that White recaptures through immediately. 'The defender of the white pawn' never names which pawn, and Nf3 was not the story. Teach the trade White invited, not a scavenger hunt of leftover pin/defender tags.

flags.quote: Taking the bishop on f3 with your e2-bishop is the strongest move because the bishop was undefended.
flags.critique: This is a recapture. Calling it winning material / an undefended bishop is how you train me to think every take-back is a tactic. wins_material and saves_piece on an equal trade are lying with a straight face.

flags.quote: Moving your d7-knight to e5 is the strongest move because your knight finds a secure outpost.
flags.critique: Secure? White plays f4 two moves later and the knight has to run or die. Outposts that a pawn can kick are not secure. Call it a central jump, not a fortress.

flags.quote: Moving your f3-bishop to e2 is the strongest move because it saves your pawn from capture.
flags.critique: Which pawn? I am staring at Ne5 hitting the bishop on f3, and you talk about an unnamed pawn (c4, if I squint). Name the square. If the point is defending hanging c4 while stepping off the knight, say that instead of 'saves your pawn.'

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to a6 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: Queenside prep for ...b5 in this Benoni/KID structure. Blank strongest-move again. I cannot tell a6 from a random waiting move.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to a4 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: This is the textbook clamp against ...b5 after ...a6. If you will not teach 'stop the break,' do not bother talking. Another empty verdict on a plan move.

flags.quote: Moving your f6-knight to d7 is a blunder, but moving your queen to a5 would be better because you pin the pawn to the rook.
flags.critique: The blunder is crowding both knights and inviting f4 against the e5-knight once f6 has left. Qa5 'because you pin the pawn to the rook' is a geometric party trick on a4–a1. Teach why Nfd7 collapses, not a pin that does not explain a 270cp swing.

flags.quote: Moving your pawn to f4 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: This is the punch of the game: kick the e5-knight, grab space, open the f-file. Your reasons are backward_pawn and pawn_shield — my own weaknesses — so they get dropped and I get silence. You have kicked_by_pawn and will not use it as a benefit for the kicker.

flags.quote: A better move would have been moving your e5-knight to c6 because it unveils an attack from your bishop on the white knight and then take a pawn.
flags.critique: The hanging-knight problem on f5 is the one sentence in this game that taught me something. Then you wreck it with a run-on that invents '...and then take a pawn' with no subject and no pawn. Do not bolt a speculative capture onto a real discovered attack on Nc3.

flags.quote: Taking the knight on e5 with your f-pawn is the strongest move because you come out a bishop ahead and it unveils an attack from your rook on the black pawn.
flags.critique: I took a knight with a pawn. After the recapture I am a knight for a pawn up, not 'a bishop ahead.' That is materialLabel mapping ~200cp to bishop while the captured unit was a knight. Also name the f5-pawn the rook hits — 'the black pawn' is noise.

flags.quote: Taking the pawn on f5 with your g-pawn is the strongest move because the pawn was undefended.
flags.critique: Recapture again sold as winning an undefended pawn (wins_material). The real story is I rip my own king shield to take back — you even tagged pawn_shield and isolated_pawn and then taught none of it. I opened the g-file on myself and you said 'free pawn.'

flags.quote: Moving your c1-bishop to f4 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: Develops onto the e5-knight and eyes the weakened dark squares after ...gxf5. Blank again. This is a developing move with a target, not a mystery 'strongest.'

flags.quote: Moving your king to h8 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: King steps off the open g-file and the a2–g8 diagonal after the shield is gone. If that is not worth a because-clause, stop calling king walks the strongest move.

flags.quote: Moving your f8-rook to g8 is a mistake, but moving your queen to e8 would be better.
flags.critique: You tagged semi_open_file — a reason that sounds like praise — then called it a mistake and offered Qe8 with zero why. I am 170cp worse and you will not say whether it is king safety, a tactic, or a better square. Bare 'would be better' is a shrug.

flags.quote: Moving your a1-rook to e1 is the strongest move.
flags.critique: Centralizing the last rook onto the e-file while pieces are hanging out on e5. Eval swings 122cp and you still have nothing to say. 'That's the one.' is wallpaper.

flags.quote: Moving your queen to e8 is a mistake, but moving your queen to d7 would be better.
flags.critique: Two plies ago you told me to play Qe8. I play it and now it is a mistake, again with no because. Either the suggestion was brittle after Rae1 or your missed-improvement template cannot explain a queen shuffle. I am not going to trust the next 'would be better' either.

flags.quote: Taking the knight on e5 with your f4-bishop is the strongest move because you pin the bishop to the king and it unveils an attack from your rook on the black pawn.
flags.critique: The knight is defended by d6 and f5, so hanging is false. 'Pin the bishop to the king' never says it is Black's g7-bishop on the e5–h8 diagonal. 'The black pawn' is f5 again, unnamed. I can tell you glued leftover tags together.

flags.quote: Moving your queen to g6 is the strongest move because you pin the pawn to the king.
flags.critique: Pinning g2 to the king is a cheap geometric hit; the queen also eyes the f5-rook and the open g-file. You burned 103cp of eval calling this strongest and taught a pin that does not win the pawn. Name squares or admit it is just queen activity.

flags.quote: You are still worse, but moving your pawn to h5 puts it at risk of attack from the white f5-rook and bishop. A better move would have been moving your a8-rook to f8 because you can likely take a rook.
flags.critique: h5 is not 'at risk' — it hangs to Rxh5+ check, forking king and bishop, 876cp. Soften that into a future attack and I miss the tactic. Then Raf8 'because you can likely take a rook' invents a capture of a rook defended by Bg4. That is the exact 'likely take' lie the review brief warned about.

suggestions.title: Stop calling recaptures winning material
suggestions.detail: wins_material currently fires when capturedSeeCp >= 80, so equal take-backs become 'the bishop was undefended' (plies 19, 28, 30, 38) and knight-for-pawn SEE of ~200 becomes materialLabel 'a bishop' (ply 27 fxe5). Suppress wins_material when the capture is recouping a just-lost unit, and describe net trades from captured type plus leftover pawns ('a knight for a pawn') instead of mapping 200cp to bishop. A 1200 notices immediately that taking back is not a tactic.

suggestions.title: Treat pawn kicks as the mover's idea
suggestions.detail: kicked_by_pawn exists only as a problem on the victim. h3 vs Bg4 and f4 vs Ne5 are the instructive moves in this game and both rendered as bare 'strongest move' (f4 even collected own pawn_shield/backward_pawn, which discourse correctly dropped, leaving silence). Add a benefit kind from move-effects when a pawn attack forces a minor piece to move or recapture, with phrase-bank lines like 'you kick the knight off e5'. That is the lesson a club player came for.

suggestions.title: Never ship 'would be better' with no why
suggestions.detail: missedImprovementSentence already has the because-slot; plies 34 and 36 hit the no-suggestedBecause branch. If contrastBenefits on the suggested line is empty, pick a structure/safety reason from suggestedEffects or withhold the SAN. Qe8 was recommended then punished two plies later with the same empty template — a 1200 will assume the coach is guessing.

suggestions.title: Raise the bar on 'you can likely take'
suggestions.detail: verifyLikelyTactics plus capture.likely produced 'then take a pawn' (ply 26) and 'you can likely take a rook' (ply 42 Raf8 vs a rook protected by Bg4). Require winning SEE on the follow-up capture, and drop the clause rather than inventing material. This is the highest-trust failure in the dump: the played-move hanging lesson on f5 was good, then the alternative lied.

suggestions.title: Do not emit a period after 'strongest move' with no reason
suggestions.detail: verdictSentence with null playedBecause produced a dozen empty strongest-move lines (g6, d5, h3, a6, a4, f4, Bf4, Kh8, Qd2, Rae1). Fall back to a weaker but true slot — development, 'it continues the plan', or a new structure motif — or downgrade the verdict to 'a good developing move' when margin is near_equal. Empty + 'That's the one.' is the template-farm cadence the brief asked to kill.

suggestions.title: Detect fianchetto, pawn breaks, and clamps
suggestions.detail: King's Indian / Benoni moves g6, Bg7, d6, c5, d5, a6, a4 all collapsed to center_control or nothing. Add cheap structure facts (fianchetto bishop, pawn break on c5/e5, d4–d5 closing the center, a4 restraining ...b5) and phrase-bank lines. Center-control hashing already makes d6 and c5 identical; a 1200 needs the named plan, not 'pressure on the center' on repeat.

suggestions.title: Put color and square on pins, saves, and defenders
suggestions.detail: Copy like 'pin the bishop to the queen', 'saves your pawn from capture', 'defender of the white pawn', 'rook on the black pawn' (plies 18, 21, 27, 37, 40) forces the learner to guess. labeledPiece/ownedPhrase already can include squares; require them for pawn and bishop, and drop pins that vanish on the forced recapture ply so Bxf3 does not teach a ghost pin on e2.

suggestions.title: Say check and fork when the pawn hangs with check
suggestions.detail: Ply 42 phrases Rxh5+ as the pawn being 'at risk of attack from the rook and bishop' instead of hanging to a check that forks king and bishop — which ply 43 then describes correctly after the fact. Prefer check/fork problem copy over generic hanging when the refutation is a checking capture. Soft 'at risk' is how you miss the only tactic that ended the game.

whatWorked: Ply 26 actually named the hanging e5-knight after f4 — the one played-move lesson that matched the board.
Castling lines on plies 8 and 15 sound like a human: king shelter plus rook toward the center.
Ply 41 Bg4 correctly taught the discovered rook hit on the e5-bishop.
Ply 43 Rxh5+ named the king-and-bishop fork; that is the tactic ply 42 should have previewed.
